summary: A 1980 revision of the Internet Message Protocol, which describes a way to send messages between hosts. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet Message Protocol describes how Message Processing Modules (MPMs) can route messages between users on connected networks. Messages have delivery instructions and may carry a separate document, while MPMs can relay them toward their destination.

subtitle: A structured system for moving messages between processing modules on connected networks.

tldr.problem: Independent message systems needed a way to exchange messages across different networks.
tldr.mechanism: Message Processing Modules route structured messages containing an identifier, delivery command and optional document over a reliable two-way communication service.
tldr.outcome: The memo specifies a general-purpose internetwork message system and is now Historic.

today: RFC 759 is Historic. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: A Message System Across Networks
sections.content:
RFC 759 describes a general-purpose system for transmitting messages between message-processing programs on hosts in different networks. It focuses on the internal mechanisms for transmission, not the user interface. The same system could connect separate message systems or serve as a message delivery system itself.

The RFC allows message documents to contain data beyond ordinary text, including objects such as drawings, facsimile images or digitized speech. Converting between this format and a local system may lose information if that local system cannot represent all the document's content.
sections.plainLanguage: This protocol lets computer message systems pass messages across network boundaries. A message can contain more than text, but a receiving system may not support every kind of content.

sections.title: Message Identity, Command and Document
sections.content:
A message normally has an identification, a command and an optional document. The identification combines the originating MPM's identifier with a transaction number. The command names a destination mailbox and operation, may include operation arguments and error information, and carries a trace of the MPMs that handled the message.

The defined operations include DELIVER and its ACKNOWLEDGE reply, PROBE and its RESPONSE reply, and CANCEL and its CANCELED reply. Several messages can be batched as a message-bag. The delivery system does not inspect the document part; its contents are defined separately.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message identifies its transaction, says where it should go and what operation to perform, and may include a document. Replies report delivery, answer mailbox checks or confirm cancellation.

sections.title: How MPMs Route Messages
sections.content:
A Message Processing Module (MPM) takes a submitted message, examines its destination and selects an outgoing link. It can deliver to a user on the same host, send to another MPM on the same network, or forward toward an MPM on another network. An MPM that lacks a direct route can send the message to a nearer MPM that knows more about the internetwork.

MPMs may act as endpoints or as relays, and a relay can pass a message between communication environments. Messages may be held temporarily, so the full path to the destination need not be available at one time. Each MPM adds a handling stamp to the trace, which can help detect routing loops and isolate faults.
sections.plainLanguage: An MPM sends a message directly when it knows the next destination. If it does not know the full route, it can pass the message to another MPM to relay it onward.

sections.title: Communication Between MPMs
sections.content:
MPMs exchange messages over a reliable, two-way communication service. The RFC requires ordered delivery, flow control, connection open and close operations, and correction of transmission errors without involving the message sender or receiver. A complete communication failure must be reported.

The RFC names TCP as an example of a transport-level protocol that can provide this service. The message protocol sits above transport and below the user-facing message programs in the protocol hierarchy described in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: MPMs need a reliable connection that delivers data in order and reports when communication fails. The RFC gives TCP as an example of a transport that can provide these services.
